title: They vaped 120 people to see if weed really melts stress. The placebo worked too.

study.citation: Cuttler, C., Proctor, M. A., Glodosky, N. C., Rahimi Azghan, R., Fisher, Z. D. G., Ghasemzadeh, H. & McLaughlin, R. J. (2026), "Multimodal examination of the acute effects of cannabis on subjective and physiological stress-related outcomes: a randomized placebo-controlled laboratory study", Neuropsychopharmacology, published online 22 August 2026

tldr: A Washington State team had 120 regular users vape placebo, 20 milligrams of THC or 40 milligrams, then tracked four different stress signals at once: everyone reported feeling calmer including the placebo group, while the body underneath was doing several contradictory things.

sections.body: Ask people why they use cannabis and stress relief lands near the top of the list. It is the reason on the dispensary shelf talker and the reason in the survey data. The trouble is that stress is not one thing you can point at. There is the feeling of being stressed, and underneath it there are separate body systems: a hormone released by the adrenal glands, sweat glands that fire in fractions of a second, a heart that speeds up. Those can move independently. Nobody had watched all of them at once while people actually got high under placebo-controlled conditions.

A team led by Carrie Cuttler at Washington State University recruited 120 adults who use cannabis regularly, 56 men, 52 women and 12 nonbinary or transgender participants. Each person was randomly assigned to vape one of three things: a placebo, a moderate dose of 20 milligrams of THC, or a high dose of 40 milligrams. Neither the participant nor the researcher running the session knew which. Three times over the visit, before vaping, five minutes after, and sixty minutes after, participants rated how stressed they felt and spat into a tube so the lab could measure cortisol. Throughout, a wristband recorded skin conductance, heart rate and heart rate variability.

Self-rated stress dropped in every condition, including placebo, which points at expectation doing the work. Cortisol fell in the first five minutes across the board, with a larger drop in the high-dose group, then climbed back between five and sixty minutes in both cannabis groups. Skin conductance responses got smaller in both cannabis groups, while the high-dose group showed more of those little sweat-gland bursts per minute at the sixty-minute mark. Heart rate ran higher on the high dose than on placebo during vaping and five minutes after. Heart rate variability showed no detectable effect.

This is the first study to put subjective stress, the hormone response, the sweat response and the cardiovascular response on the same clock in one placebo-controlled session. Splitting the claim into pieces is what makes it interesting. The calm people reported looks like something they brought with them. The body did respond to THC, and it responded in more than one direction at the same time, quieting some stress channels while pushing the heart harder. The authors point out what that means for the very large number of people using cannabis as a coping tool.

Everyone in the room was already a regular user, so tolerance is baked into every number and a first-timer might look completely different. It was a single lab session, which says nothing about what weeks or years of use do to a stress system. Blinding is genuinely hard here, since experienced users often notice when they are high. The abstract reports which comparisons reached statistical significance without the size of each effect, so treat these as directions rather than magnitudes. Two of the authors disclose receiving study-related materials from Storz and Bickel, a vaporizer manufacturer.

terms.def: The body's main stress hormone, released by the adrenal glands when something demanding happens, and measurable in a sample of spit.
How easily a tiny electrical current crosses the skin, which changes within seconds as sweat glands fire, making it a fast readout of physical arousal.
When believing you took a drug produces part or all of the change you feel, whether or not the drug was actually in the dose.

takeaways: People felt calmer after vaping THC, and the placebo group felt calmer by about the same amount, which is what an expectancy effect looks like.
The body did react to THC, in opposite directions at once: a bigger early cortisol drop and smaller sweat responses alongside a faster heart rate.
If you use cannabis to take the edge off, the edge coming off may be partly the ritual and the belief, and your cardiovascular system is not going along with the calm.

quiz.q: Self-rated stress dropped in the placebo condition by roughly as much as in the THC conditions. What does that pattern most directly suggest?
choices: Much of the felt calm came from expectation and the situation rather than from the drug
The stress ratings were measured incorrectly
quiz.why: A placebo group exists precisely to catch this. If the people who got nothing active report the same improvement as the people who got 40 milligrams, then the improvement cannot be credited to the molecule. Sitting down, being taken care of, going through the ritual of vaping and believing something is coming will all move a self-report. That is the whole reason the comparison group is there.

quiz.q: Why did the researchers measure cortisol, skin conductance and heart rate instead of just asking people how stressed they felt?
choices: Because the equipment was available and it made the study look thorough
Because those systems can move independently, so the feeling and the physiology can disagree
Because cortisol is the only real measure of stress
quiz.why: Stress is a bundle of loosely connected processes. A hormone response can be dampened while the heart speeds up, and neither has to match what a person says on a rating scale. That is exactly what happened here. Measuring several channels on the same clock is what let the team see that the calm people reported and the state of their body were telling different stories.

quiz.q: What is the biggest reason to be careful generalizing this result to the population at large?
choices: The study had no placebo group
Only 120 people took part, which is too few for any conclusion
Every participant was already a regular cannabis user, so tolerance shapes every measurement
quiz.why: The design is solid: randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, with 120 participants and doses in the range people actually use. The limit is who was in the room. Regular users have adapted cannabinoid systems, and their hormone and heart responses to a given dose can differ from someone who rarely uses. This tells you about the stress physiology of experienced users, and an occasional user remains an open question.
